analysis.investment_thesis: Arvind Limited is a 128-year-old textile conglomerate with near-zero revenue growth (0.4% CAGR over 9 years) and an ROE of just 9.3% — well below my 15% minimum for any meaningful position. The structural tailwinds of India's growth story are largely bypassing this business, and at 24x earnings, the market is pricing in optimism that the fundamentals do not yet justify.
key_strengths: Consistent debt reduction: borrowings nearly halved from INR 2,640 Cr (2020) to INR 1,537 Cr (2025), bringing D/E to a safe 0.39
Unbroken positive OCF across all 5 years (average ~700 Cr), indicating the core textile business is cash-generative
Capex surge to INR 535 Cr in FY25 (vs. 278 Cr prior year) signals management intent on growth — CWIP up to 331 Cr, potential inflection ahead
key_risks: Chronically weak returns: ROE at 9.3% and ROCE at 13% — capital is not being deployed effectively for shareholders
Promoter holding of only 39.5% is below my 50% comfort threshold — signals limited skin-in-the-game and potential for further dilution
Conglomerate discount risk: scattered presence in textiles, automotive, water treatment, real estate, and telecom dilutes management focus and makes valuation opaque
red_flags: Revenue in FY2025 (INR 8,329 Cr) is barely above FY2016 (INR 8,011 Cr) — 9-year CAGR of 0.4% is a serious red flag for any growth-oriented investor
EBITDA CAGR of -3.1% over 9 years means the business is actually shrinking in real terms
Net Profit swung to a loss in FY2021 and remains volatile — earnings quality is poor for a company of this vintage
FCF declining sharply to INR 280 Cr in FY25 as heavy capex bites; returns on this new investment are unproven
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Arvind is a classic Indian textile conglomerate that has failed to compound wealth. Revenue was INR 8,011 Cr in 2016 and is INR 8,329 Cr in 2025 — a decade of essentially standing still. This is not a company riding India's consumption boom; it is treading water within it. The ROE of 9.3% is deeply unsatisfying — I need to see at least 15-20% to get excited, and Arvind has never come close on a sustained basis. The EBITDA CAGR of -3.1% over nine years tells you that even the operating earnings power has eroded, not grown.

The one silver lining is the FY25 capex surge (INR 535 Cr, up from INR 278 Cr in FY24) and the rising CWIP, which suggests the Lalbhai family is reinvesting in capacity — possibly in technical textiles and advanced materials, which carry better margins. But the promoter holding of only 39.5% concerns me deeply; I want promoters who are all-in on their own businesses. At 24x earnings for a near-zero-growth business, the market is valuing this on hope rather than evidence. I would rather deploy capital into financial services or consumer companies compounding at 18-25% than wait for a textile conglomerate to find its mojo.
